raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the mortality benefit of defibrillator therapy while avoiding transvenous leads, venous access, and direct endocardial contact. The foundational human studies established a left lateral pulse generator and parasternal subcutaneous electrode configuration, demonstrated reliable defibrillation, and framed the key trade-off: an extravascular system capable of high-energy shocks but unable to provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or conventional antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [1]. Subsequent IDE, EFFORTLESS, pooled, and long-term registry data confirmed high conversion efficacy for induced and spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, low electrode failure, and absence of S-ICD-related endocarditis, while identifying early infection/erosion and inappropriate shocks as the principal complications [2-6].

Patient selection remains central. The S-ICD is most attractive for patients with an ICD indication who do not need pacing: younger patients facing decades of lead exposure, patients with limited venous access, prior device infection, congenital or inherited arrhythmia syndromes, or high risk from transvenous lead extraction. Contemporary post-approval experience broadened the evidence base beyond early, relatively young cohorts, showing feasible implantation across diverse U.S. practice with high acute conversion success and acceptable early complications [7]. One-year post-approval results and UNTOUCHED, a primary-prevention trial in patients with low ejection fraction, showed that modern programming and sensing algorithms can yield low inappropriate shock rates even in a heart-failure population more typical of contemporary ICD practice [8,9].

Randomized comparative evidence has clarified the S-ICD’s role. PRAETORIAN demonstrated noninferiority of S-ICD versus transvenous ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks in patients without pacing indications [10]. Secondary analyses showed qualitatively different complication profiles: fewer lead-related and systemic infectious complications with S-ICD, but more pocket-related issues such as bleeding or discomfort [11]. PRAETORIAN appropriate-therapy analyses also highlighted the expected limitation: ATP in transvenous ICDs can terminate some monomorphic ventricular tachycardias without shocks, whereas S-ICD patients require shock therapy for sustained ventricular arrhythmias [12]. ATLAS, enriched for younger or lead-complication-prone patients, similarly found fewer perioperative lead-related complications with S-ICD, at the cost of more early pocket pain and a nonsignificant trend toward more inappropriate shocks [13]. Observational comparative studies support similar survival and shock efficacy when patients are appropriately selected [14,15].

The main technical challenges are sensing and shock vector optimization. Because the device senses far-field subcutaneous electrograms, preimplant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory; failure is more likely with wide QRS complexes, hypertrophy, bundle-branch block, and dynamic repolarization changes [16]. Algorithms have evolved from morphology discrimination to SMART Pass high-pass filtering, reducing T-wave oversensing without compromising ventricular arrhythmia detection [17,18]. Nevertheless, inappropriate shocks persist from myopotential noise, T-wave oversensing, low QRS amplitude, air entrapment, and vector instability, emphasizing careful screening, exercise testing in selected patients, and early postimplant interrogation [19,20].

Implant technique has also matured. The original three-incision subcutaneous approach has largely given way to two-incision and intermuscular generator placement between serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi, improving cosmesis, stability, and defibrillation vectors [21,22]. Multicenter data suggest intermuscular two-incision implantation lowers shock impedance and acute defibrillation-test failure [23]. Whether routine defibrillation testing can be omitted remains debated. Early single-center data cautioned that failed testing was not rare [24,25], whereas more recent real-world and national cohort data suggest selective omission may be safe in standard-risk recipients when implant position and impedance are favorable [26].

Special populations illustrate both advantages and boundaries. Pediatric and congenital-heart cohorts benefit from avoiding venous occlusion and intracardiac leads but have higher screening-failure rates and size-related pocket concerns [27-29]. In adults with progressive cardiomyopathy, later need for CRT, bradycardia pacing, or ATP may require conversion to a transvenous or hybrid system. Future development is therefore focused on modular extravascular therapy: a leadless pacemaker communicating wirelessly with an S-ICD has shown promising early performance, including ATP delivery while preserving the extravascular defibrillator lead strategy [30]. Overall, the S-ICD is now an evidence-based alternative to transvenous ICDs for patients who need defibrillation but not pacing; optimal outcomes depend on disciplined selection, meticulous implantation, contemporary programming, and shared decision-making about shocks, lead avoidance, and future pacing needs.
